questions.title: Cytopathology: diagnosis from isolated cells
questions.question: The diagnosis of disease by examination of isolated cells in body fluids is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Molecular pathology examines a disease at the level of DNA, RNA or protein molecules, not isolated whole cells in a fluid sample -- a different scale of examination from what this question describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Microbiology studies microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites) themselves, not the patient's own cells shed into a body fluid -- a different subject of examination entirely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Histpoathology" (histopathology) examines an intact tissue specimen removed by a surgeon, not isolated cells in a fluid sample -- the distinguishing fact here is tissue architecture versus individual cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Immunology studies the immune system and its responses, not the diagnostic examination of isolated cells in body fluids.
explanations.E: Correct. Cytopathology (cytological diagnosis) examines isolated cells shed or aspirated from the body -- exfoliated cells in sputum, urine or CSF, or a fine-needle aspirate -- rather than an intact tissue specimen. It is used for screening and rapid sampling, complementary to but distinct from histopathology, which instead examines a removed piece of tissue with its architecture preserved.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify cytopathology as the branch of pathological diagnosis that examines isolated cells in body fluids.

questions.title: Histopathology: diagnosis from tissue sections
questions.question: The diagnosis of disease from the examination of tissue sections is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Microbiology studies microorganisms themselves, not the diagnostic examination of tissue sections removed from a patient.
explanations.B: Correct. Histopathological diagnosis examines a tissue specimen (a biopsy) removed by a surgeon, under the microscope. It is considered the definitive method for diagnosing most diseases. This is because it preserves tissue architecture and shows how cells relate to one another, not just isolated cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hematology studies blood and blood-forming tissues and their disorders, not the general diagnostic examination of tissue sections.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Immunology studies the immune system and its responses, not tissue-section diagnosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cytopathology examines isolated cells (a smear or fluid sample), not an intact tissue specimen with its architecture preserved -- the opposite of what this question describes.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify histopathology as the definitive diagnostic method, based on examination of a tissue specimen.

questions.title: Gross pathology: naked-eye observation
questions.question: The observation of the pathological changes of organs or tissues by the naked eye is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Molecular pathology examines disease at the molecular (DNA/RNA/protein) level, not by naked-eye inspection of an organ or tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Experimental pathology studies disease mechanisms through controlled experiments (often in animal or cell models), not the routine naked-eye description of a diseased specimen.
explanations.C: Correct. Gross (morphological) pathology is the naked-eye description of a diseased organ or specimen -- its size, shape, colour, cut surface and consistency -- performed before any microscopic step. It is read first in the diagnostic workflow, giving an overall picture that the later microscopic examination then refines.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Histopathology is microscopic examination of a tissue specimen, not naked-eye observation -- the opposite scale of examination from what this question describes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Clinical pathology broadly covers laboratory diagnosis from patient samples (blood chemistry, microbiology, etc.), not specifically the naked-eye description of an organ's gross appearance.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify gross (morphological) pathology as the naked-eye description of a diseased organ or specimen.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: gross pathology"

questions.title: Prognosis: predicting disease course
questions.question: The prediction of how a patient's disease will progress is called:

explanations.A: Correct. Prognosis is the prediction of how a patient's disease will progress -- its fate or outcome, whether regression (a good fate) or progression with complications (a bad fate). It looks forward from the current state of disease, distinct from pathogenesis (the mechanism that already produced the lesion) and etiology (the original cause).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aetiology is the cause of a disease, the starting point of the causal chain, not a prediction of what happens next.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diagnosis is identifying what disease a patient has, not predicting how it will progress once identified.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pathogenesis is the mechanism by which a disease's lesion was produced -- a backward-looking, mechanistic term, not the forward-looking prediction that "prognosis" names.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Complications are specific bad outcomes that may occur during a disease's course; they are one possible content of a poor prognosis, not the general term for predicting the disease's course itself.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define prognosis as the forward-looking prediction of a disease's future course, distinct from pathogenesis and aetiology.

questions.title: Pathogenesis: the mechanism of lesion production
questions.question: The steps or mechanisms of production of the lesion of a disease is termed:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Morphology is the study of an organism's or lesion's structure/form, not specifically the steps by which the lesion was produced.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diagnosis is identifying what disease is present, not the mechanistic steps that produced its lesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prognosis is a forward-looking prediction of how the disease will progress, the opposite direction from the backward-looking mechanism this question asks about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aetiology names the cause that started the disease process, not the subsequent mechanistic steps that turned that cause into a lesion -- pathogenesis picks up where aetiology leaves off.
explanations.E: Correct. Pathogenesis means the steps or mechanism of production of the lesion of a disease -- the causal chain connecting a cause (etiology) to the structural change (lesion) eventually seen. It answers "how" the disease produced its damage, distinct from "why" it started (aetiology) or "what happens next" (prognosis).

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define pathogenesis as the mechanism producing a disease's lesion, distinct from prognosis and aetiology.

questions.title: Immunohistochemistry: antibody-enzyme tissue staining
questions.question: The use of antibodies linked chemically to enzymes to visualize specific substances in tissue sections is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Molecular pathology broadly covers DNA/RNA/protein-level disease analysis; it does not specifically name the antibody-enzyme conjugate technique this question describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cytopathology examines isolated cells in fluid samples; it is a different diagnostic branch from a specific tissue-staining technique.
explanations.C: Correct. Immunohistochemistry links an antibody chemically to an enzyme (most commonly the immunoperoxidase technique) to bind and visualise a specific substance within tissue sections. That substance is typically a cytoplasmic protein, enzyme or hormone. The technique is commonly used to detect tumour markers, identifying what a tumour is expressing beyond routine staining.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Immunofluorescence (misspelled here as "Immunofulrescence") also uses labelled antibodies, but the label is a fluorescent dye visualised under UV/fluorescence microscopy, not an enzyme conjugate producing a visible colour reaction -- a different detection chemistry from what this question describes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Histochemistry is the broader study of chemical composition and reactions within tissue using various stains, not specifically the antibody-enzyme conjugate method this question names.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify immunohistochemistry as the antibody-enzyme conjugate technique for visualising specific substances in tissue sections.

questions.title: Formalin 10% as tissue fixative
questions.question: To preserve a specimen removed from the body from autolysis we add fixative to the tissue consisting of:

explanations.A: Correct. The standard fixative for a tissue specimen is formaldehyde solution at 10% concentration (formalin 10%). It preserves the specimen from decay and autolysis. It also stabilises tissue integrity for the histopathological examination that follows.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ethyl alcohol is used as a fixative for cytological smears, not for tissue blocks, and 70% is not the concentration taught for either specimen type in this teaching set.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Formalin 100% is not the standard working concentration taught for tissue fixation; the teaching value is specifically 10%, a diluted working solution, not full-strength formaldehyde.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Formalin 50% is not the standard concentration taught for tissue fixation; the correct working concentration is 10%.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ethyl alcohol 95% (like 70%) is the fixative used for cytological smears, not tissue blocks, and this question specifically asks about the tissue-specimen fixative.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify formalin 10% as the standard fixative for a tissue specimen, preventing autolysis before histopathological examination.

questions.title: Absorption as critical for therapeutic plasma concentration
questions.question: Which of the following steps is most critical to achieve a therapeutic drug concentration in plasma?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Distribution moves an already-absorbed drug from blood into tissues; it presupposes the drug already reached the blood, which is exactly the step absorption governs and this question is asking about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Elimination (excretion) removes drug from the body after it has acted; it determines how long a concentration lasts, not whether a therapeutic concentration is reached in the first place.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Metabolism biotransforms a drug, usually reducing its active concentration; it happens after the drug has entered the body, not as the step that determines whether it gets there at all.
explanations.D: Correct. Absorption -- a drug's movement from the site of administration into the bloodstream -- is the pharmacokinetic step most critical for achieving a therapeutic plasma drug concentration. A drug that never reaches the blood in adequate amount cannot act, however well it later distributes, metabolises or is excreted. That is why absorption, not any of the three later phases, is singled out here.

questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: State that absorption is the pharmacokinetic step that determines whether a therapeutic plasma concentration is reached at all.

questions.title: Generic (approved) drug name
questions.question: What is the approved (generic) name of a drug?

options.A: the name used to market the drug
options.B: a precise description of the drug's chemical composition and molecular structure
options.C: a name that is protected by copyright
options.D: The official drug name assigned by the manufacturer and approved by the local regulatory authority.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The name used to market a drug is its brand (proprietary/trade) name, owned by a specific manufacturer -- the opposite of the regulator-approved, non-proprietary generic name this question asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A precise description of a drug's chemical composition and molecular structure is its chemical name, a distinct third naming category alongside the generic and brand names.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A copyright-protected name is characteristic of a brand/trade name, not a generic name, which is specifically not owned by any one company.
explanations.D: Correct. The generic (approved/official) name is the official drug name assigned to and approved by the local regulatory authority -- not protected by any one company, distinct from a chemical name (a structural description) and a brand name (a specific manufacturer's marketing name for the same drug, e.g. Valium for the generic diazepam).

questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Identify a drug's generic/official name as its regulator-approved, non-proprietary name, distinct from its chemical and brand names.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: The official drug name assigned by the manufacturer and approved by the local regulatory authority."

questions.title: ADME: the pharmacokinetic phase sequence
questions.question: The most common sequence of pharmacokinetics phases a drug may pass through is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Administration and inhalation are ways a drug is given (a route), not pharmacokinetic phases themselves; the standard sequence begins only once the drug starts moving through the body, at absorption.
explanations.B: Correct. The standard sequence of pharmacokinetic phases is absorption (entry into the bloodstream), distribution (movement into tissues), metabolism (biotransformation) and excretion (removal from the body) -- abbreviated ADME. This is the reference order taught for how a drug's course through the body is organised.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Disintegration (a pharmaceutical/formulation step) and expiration are not recognised pharmacokinetic phases; the standard sequence is absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Formulation is how a drug product is manufactured, not a pharmacokinetic phase the drug passes through inside the body; substituting it for distribution breaks the correct ADME sequence.

questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: State the correct ADME order of pharmacokinetic phases, rejecting distractor sequences that substitute non-pharmacokinetic steps.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion."

questions.title: Definition of pharmacology
questions.question: The definition of pharmacology is:

options.A: the study of history of drugs
options.B: the study of the formulation of drugs
options.C: The study of pharmacy (the preparation and development of drugs).
options.D: the study of drugs, including their actions and effects in living systems

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pharmacology is not defined as the history of drugs; a historical account may be part of an introduction to the field, but the discipline itself is defined by studying drug action, not drug history.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The formulation of drugs (how a dosage form is manufactured) is part of pharmaceutics/pharmacy, not the definition of pharmacology itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes pharmacy, not pharmacology -- pharmacy is the preparation and development of drugs, a distinct discipline from pharmacology, which studies what drugs do once given.
explanations.D: Correct. Pharmacology is the study of drugs, including their actions and effects in living systems -- distinct from pharmacy, which is the preparation and development of drugs. This distinction (pharmacology studies drug action; pharmacy prepares the drug) is the exact contrast the distractors in this question are built to test.

questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Define pharmacology as the study of drugs' actions and effects, distinct from pharmacy.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: the study of drugs, including their actions and effects in living systems"

questions.title: Insulin: a drug from both human and animal sources
questions.question: Select the drug from both human and animal sources:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Morphine is sourced from the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum), a plant source only -- it has no separate animal-derived or human/recombinant version.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Iodine is a mineral/elemental source, not a drug obtained from both animal and human sources.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cod liver oil is an animal product only; it has no human or recombinant-technology source, unlike insulin.
explanations.D: Correct. Insulin is obtained from more than one source category at once: originally from animal pancreas (bovine/porcine), and now also as a human-sequence molecule produced by recombinant DNA technology in microbes such as E. coli or yeast -- making it the worked teaching example of a drug spanning both an animal source and a human-sequence source.

questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Identify insulin as a drug obtained from both animal and human/recombinant sources, distinct from single-source drug examples.

questions.title: Oral route gives the lowest serum drug concentration
questions.question: One of the following routes of medication administration would provide the lowest serum drug concentration?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Intravenous administration bypasses absorption entirely -- 100% of the dose reaches the blood immediately -- giving the highest, not lowest, achieved serum concentration among these routes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Intrathecal administration delivers a drug directly into the cerebrospinal fluid, bypassing the gut and first-pass metabolism; it is not the route giving the lowest serum concentration among these options.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intramuscular administration is generally well and fairly completely absorbed into the bloodstream, giving a higher achieved serum concentration for an equivalent dose than oral administration.
explanations.D: Correct. Oral administration is subject to incomplete absorption across the gut wall. It also undergoes first-pass hepatic metabolism before any drug reaches systemic circulation. Together these two losses give oral the lowest achieved serum concentration among the routes compared here (IV, intrathecal, intramuscular, oral) for an equivalent dose.

questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Rank oral administration as giving the lowest serum concentration among IV/intrathecal/intramuscular/oral routes for an equivalent dose, and explain why (incomplete absorption plus first-pass metabolism).

questions.title: Calcium influx in irreversible cell injury
questions.question: Influx of which of the following ions plays a major role in irreversible cell injury:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Potassium characteristically leaks out of an injured cell (loss of the ion gradient normally maintained by the sodium pump), rather than being the ion whose influx drives irreversible damage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Iron overload is associated with its own specific injury mechanisms (e.g. free-radical generation via the Fenton reaction) in particular clinical settings, but it is not the ion named as the general mechanism of irreversible cell injury taught here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sodium does accumulate inside an injured cell (via sodium-pump failure, causing swelling), but it is calcium, not sodium, whose rise activates the degradative enzyme cascade that specifically marks irreversible injury.
explanations.D: Correct. Rising intracellular calcium is the ion influx that plays the major role in irreversible cell injury. Once elevated, calcium activates phospholipase, proteases, ATPase and endonucleases. This degradative enzyme cascade is what converts a reversibly-injured cell into one with irreversible damage and death.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify calcium influx as the ion movement that plays the major role in converting reversible cell injury into irreversible injury.

questions.title: Calcium as the mechanism of membrane damage in ischaemia
questions.question: The major mechanism of plasma membrane damage in ischaemia is:

options.D: Increased ca ions in the cytoplasm

explanations.A: Incorrect. Intracellular pH does fall in ischaemia (from anaerobic glycolysis and lactate accumulation), but this is a metabolic consequence, not the major mechanism that directly damages the plasma membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reduced aerobic respiration is the upstream cause of ATP depletion in ischaemia, but it is calcium's own downstream enzyme activation, not reduced respiration itself, that is the major mechanism of membrane damage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sodium accumulates (increases), not decreases, intracellularly during ischaemia, because ATP depletion disables the sodium pump -- this option both reverses the direction of the sodium change and names the wrong ion for membrane damage.
explanations.D: Correct. Increased calcium ions in the cytoplasm are the major mechanism of plasma membrane damage in ischaemia. Calcium, normally kept low by energy-dependent transport, rises when that transport fails. The rise activates phospholipase, which directly degrades membrane phospholipids -- the specific step that damages the plasma membrane itself.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that rising cytoplasmic calcium, via phospholipase activation, is the major mechanism of plasma membrane damage in ischaemia.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Increased ca ions in the cytoplasm"

questions.title: Nicotinic ACh receptor as the time-scale exception
questions.question: All of the following receptors match with their time scale except:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this pairing is correct. Muscarinic ACh receptors are G-protein coupled (metabotropic) receptors, whose response unfolds over seconds, so this match is accurate.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is the exception (wrongly matched pairing). Nicotinic ACh receptors are ligand-gated ion channels (ionotropic), the fastest receptor superfamily, acting within milliseconds -- not days. "Days" would only fit the slowest, intracellular/nuclear-receptor category, so pairing the fast, directly channel-linked nicotinic receptor with a days-long time scale is the mismatch this question isolates.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception -- this pairing is correct. Estrogen receptors are intracellular/nuclear receptors, whose response (via new gene transcription) unfolds over hours to days, so "Hours" is a reasonable match on this scale.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this pairing is correct. The insulin receptor is a tyrosine-kinase-linked receptor, whose response unfolds over minutes, matching the given time scale.

questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Rank the four receptor superfamilies by response time scale (ion-channel-linked fastest, intracellular slowest), and identify the nicotinic ACh receptor as ionotropic (milliseconds), not days-scale.

questions.title: Muscarinic and adrenergic receptors are G-protein coupled
questions.question: Muscarinic ACh receptors and adrenergic receptors are associated with which of the following?

options.B: Transmembrane receptors with enzymatic cytosolic domains
options.D: Intracellular receptors for lipid soluble ligands

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ligand-gated ion channels are the nicotinic (not muscarinic) acetylcholine receptor's structural family; muscarinic and adrenergic receptors are a different superfamily entirely.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transmembrane receptors with enzymatic cytosolic domains describes the tyrosine-kinase-linked family (e.g. the insulin receptor), not muscarinic or adrenergic receptors.
explanations.C: Correct. Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and adrenergic receptors are both G-protein coupled (metabotropic) receptors. Ligand binding activates a G-protein, which regulates an effector enzyme and changes a second-messenger concentration. This unfolds over a response time scale of seconds, slower than a directly-linked ion channel.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intracellular receptors for lipid-soluble ligands describes the nuclear-receptor family (steroid/thyroid hormone receptors), not the membrane-bound muscarinic and adrenergic receptors.

questions.topic: Drug receptors, signaling mechanisms and drug action
questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Identify muscarinic and adrenergic receptors as G-protein coupled receptors.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: G-protein coupled receptors"

questions.title: Insulin receptor: a tyrosine-kinase-linked receptor
questions.question: Insulin at the insulin receptor interacts with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A ligand-activated (ligand-gated) ion channel is the nicotinic-receptor family's mechanism, not the insulin receptor's -- insulin does not act by directly opening an ion channel.
explanations.B: Correct. The insulin receptor is a tyrosine-kinase-linked receptor: it has an extracellular domain for insulin binding and a cytoplasmic domain with intrinsic tyrosine kinase enzymatic activity. Insulin binding stimulates this enzyme, phosphorylating target proteins on tyrosine residues to produce the cell's response, and the intracellular signal can outlast insulin's own binding.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intracellular nuclear receptors bind lipid-soluble ligands that cross the cell membrane directly (steroid/thyroid hormones); insulin is a peptide hormone that instead binds a cell-surface receptor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. G-protein-coupled receptors act through a G-protein and a second messenger; the insulin receptor instead has its own intrinsic tyrosine kinase enzymatic activity, a structurally and mechanistically different receptor family.

questions.topic: Drug receptors, signaling mechanisms and drug action
questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Identify the insulin receptor as a tyrosine-kinase-linked receptor, the worked example of this superfamily.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Receptor-activated tyrosine kinase"

questions.title: Glutamate acts on a ligand-gated ion channel
questions.question: One of the following interacts with ligand-gated ion channels:

explanations.A: Correct. Glutamate is a ligand for a ligand-gated ion channel (an ionotropic receptor). Binding directly opens the channel, producing a fast response within milliseconds. This is the same structural mechanism as the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Epinephrine acts at adrenergic receptors, which are G-protein coupled, not ligand-gated ion channels.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Steroids act at intracellular/nuclear receptors, since they are lipid-soluble and cross the cell membrane directly -- a structurally and mechanistically different, much slower pathway from a ligand-gated ion channel.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Insulin acts at a tyrosine-kinase-linked receptor, not a ligand-gated ion channel.

questions.topic: Drug receptors, signaling mechanisms and drug action
questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Identify glutamate as a ligand acting on a ligand-gated ion channel, among ligands representing the other three receptor superfamilies.

questions.title: cAMP as a G-protein coupled receptor second messenger
questions.question: Tick the second messenger of the G-protein-coupled (metabotropic) receptor:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adenylyl cyclase is the effector enzyme a G-protein activates; it produces cAMP from ATP, but the enzyme itself is not the second messenger.
explanations.B: Correct. Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) is one of the well-established second messengers of a G-protein coupled receptor. Ligand binding activates a G-protein, which regulates adenylyl cyclase. This changes intracellular cAMP concentration, producing the downstream cellular response.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sodium ions are the signal carrier for a ligand-gated ion channel (e.g. the nicotinic receptor), not the second-messenger system of a G-protein coupled receptor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Phospholipase C, like adenylyl cyclase, is an effector enzyme a G-protein can regulate (producing IP3 and DAG as the actual second messengers); the enzyme itself is not the second messenger.

questions.topic: Drug receptors, signaling mechanisms and drug action
questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Identify cAMP as a second messenger of G-protein coupled receptors, distinct from the effector enzymes (adenylyl cyclase, phospholipase C) that produce second messengers.

questions.title: GDP is not a G-protein second messenger
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a second messenger associated with G proteins?

explanations.A: Incorrect as the answer -- IP3 (inositol triphosphate) IS a well-established second messenger, produced when a G-protein activates phospholipase C.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the answer -- cAMP IS a well-established second messenger, produced when a G-protein activates adenylyl cyclase.
explanations.C: Correct. GDP is NOT a second messenger; it is the inactive-state nucleotide bound to the G-protein's alpha subunit before the receptor is activated. On ligand binding, GDP is exchanged for GTP, which activates the G-protein to regulate its effector -- GDP itself is the resting-state marker the G-protein carries, not a downstream signal the receptor produces.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer -- DAG (diacylglycerol) IS a well-established second messenger, produced alongside IP3 when a G-protein activates phospholipase C.

questions.topic: Drug receptors, signaling mechanisms and drug action
questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Identify GDP as the G-protein's own inactive-state nucleotide, not a second messenger, distinct from the well-established second messengers cAMP, IP3 and DAG.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: GDP"; also confirmed by Lecture 4's own printed answer key, p.24 ("Answer b) GDP")

questions.title: hsp90 and intracellular receptor signalling
questions.question: Which of the following signaling mechanisms can involve heat-shock protein (hsp90)?

options.C: Intracellular receptors for lipid soluble ligands

explanations.A: Incorrect. G-protein coupled receptors signal through a G-protein and a second messenger; hsp90 is not part of this membrane-receptor mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ligand-gated ion channels signal by directly opening an ion channel on ligand binding; hsp90 plays no role in this fast, membrane-confined mechanism.
explanations.C: Correct. Intracellular (nuclear) receptors bind lipid-soluble ligands (steroid hormones, thyroid hormone, vitamin D) that cross the cell membrane directly. In the resting state, heat shock protein 90 (hsp90) is bound to the receptor; when the ligand binds, hsp90 dissociates and the receptor-ligand complex translocates to the nucleus to bind a DNA response element and alter gene transcription.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Transmembrane receptors" broadly covers ion-channel, G-protein-coupled and tyrosine-kinase-linked receptors -- none of which involve hsp90, which is specific to the intracellular/nuclear-receptor mechanism.

questions.topic: Drug receptors, signaling mechanisms and drug action
questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: State hsp90's role as the chaperone that dissociates from an intracellular receptor on lipid-soluble ligand binding, before nuclear translocation.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Intracellular receptors for lipid soluble ligands"

questions.title: Drug receptor macromolecule types
questions.question: With reference to drug receptors, which of the following is true?

options.A: Receptor-mediated responses to drugs usually remain constant over time, even in the continued presence of the agonist
options.B: Pure pharmacologic antagonists bind to receptors and directly alter the receptors' function
options.C: They include regulatory proteins, enzymes, transport proteins and structural proteins
options.D: The total number of receptors is unrelated to the maximal effect of a drug

explanations.A: Incorrect. Receptor-mediated responses commonly change over time with continued agonist presence (e.g. receptor desensitisation or downregulation), rather than remaining constant -- the opposite of what this option claims.
explanations.B: Incorrect. By definition, a pure pharmacologic antagonist binds a receptor with affinity but has no efficacy of its own and does not directly alter the receptor's function -- it acts only by occupying the site and preventing an agonist from binding.
explanations.C: Correct. Receptor macromolecules are drawn from several structural classes, not exclusively dedicated signalling proteins. Regulatory proteins, enzymes, transport proteins and structural proteins can all serve as drug receptors. This is why "receptor" in pharmacology names a functional role, not one fixed molecular family.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The total number of receptors available is directly related to the maximal effect a drug can produce (e.g. via receptor reserve and spare receptors) -- receptor number is not unrelated to maximal effect.

questions.topic: Drug receptors, signaling mechanisms and drug action
questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Recognise that receptor macromolecules are drawn from several structural classes (regulatory proteins, enzymes, transport proteins, structural proteins), not exclusively dedicated signalling proteins.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: They include regulatory proteins, enzymes, transport proteins and structural proteins"
